text: On receipt of a request under section 6, the Central Public Information Officer or State Public Information Officer shall, as expeditiously as possible, and in any case within thirty days of the receipt of the request, either provide the information on payment of such fee as may be prescribed or reject the request for any of the reasons specified in sections 8 and 9.

Where the information sought in an RTI request concerns the life or liberty of a person, the Public Information Officer must provide it within forty-eight hours of receiving the request, instead of the usual thirty days.

To file an RTI request, a person must make a request in writing or through electronic means, accompanied by the prescribed fee, to the Central Public Information Officer or State Public Information Officer of the concerned public authority, or to the Central or State Assistant Public Information Officer. The request must specify the particulars of the information sought.

An RTI application can be written in English, Hindi, or the official language of the area in which the application is being made. Where the request cannot be made in writing, the Public Information Officer shall render all reasonable assistance to the person making the request orally to reduce it in writing.

An applicant making a request for information shall not be required to give any reason for requesting the information or any other personal details except those that may be necessary for contacting him.

An application sent to the wrong public authority is transferred, not rejected. Where the information is held by another public authority, or is more closely connected with that authority's functions, the authority that received the application shall transfer it, or the relevant part of it, to the correct authority and inform the applicant immediately. The transfer shall be made as soon as practicable, and in no case later than five days from the date of receipt.
If the Public Information Officer fails to give a decision on the request for information within the period specified in sub-section (1), the officer shall be deemed to have refused the request.

Where a decision is taken to provide the information on payment of further fees representing the cost of providing it, the Public Information Officer shall send an intimation giving the details of the fees and calculations, requesting the applicant to deposit the fees. The period between sending this intimation and the applicant paying the fees is excluded when calculating the thirty-day period under sub-section (1). The intimation must also inform the applicant of their right to review the fee or form of access decision, including appellate authority details, time limits and process.

Where access to information is provided in printed or electronic format, the applicant shall pay such fee as prescribed. However, this fee shall be reasonable, and no fee shall be charged from persons below the poverty line as determined by the appropriate Government.

Notwithstanding sub-section (5), the person making the request shall be provided the information free of charge if the public authority fails to comply with the time limits specified in sub-section (1).

Where a request has been rejected under sub-section (1), the Public Information Officer shall communicate to the person making the request: the reasons for such rejection, the period within which an appeal against the rejection may be preferred, and the particulars of the appellate authority.

Where access to a record or part of it is to be provided and the person to whom access is to be provided is sensorily disabled, the Public Information Officer shall provide assistance to enable access to the information, including such assistance as may be appropriate for the inspection.
Before taking any decision under sub-section (1), the Public Information Officer shall take into consideration the representation made by a third party under section 11.

Information shall ordinarily be provided in the form in which it is sought, unless doing so would disproportionately divert the resources of the public authority or would be detrimental to the safety or preservation of the record in question.

There shall be no obligation to give any citizen information, disclosure of which would prejudicially affect the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security, strategic, scientific or economic interests of the State, relation with foreign State, or lead to incitement of an offence.

There shall be no obligation to give any citizen information which has been expressly forbidden to be published by any court of law or tribunal, or the disclosure of which may constitute contempt of court.
There shall be no obligation to give any citizen information the disclosure of which would cause a breach of privilege of Parliament or the State Legislature.

There shall be no obligation to give any citizen information including commercial confidence, trade secrets or intellectual property, the disclosure of which would harm the competitive position of a third party, unless the competent authority is satisfied that larger public interest warrants disclosure.

There shall be no obligation to give any citizen information available to a person in his fiduciary relationship, unless the competent authority is satisfied that the larger public interest warrants disclosure.
There shall be no obligation to give any citizen information received in confidence from a foreign Government.

There shall be no obligation to give any citizen information the disclosure of which would endanger the life or physical safety of any person, or identify the source of information or assistance given in confidence for law enforcement or security purposes.
There shall be no obligation to give any citizen information which would impede the process of investigation or apprehension or prosecution of offenders.

There shall be no obligation to give any citizen cabinet papers, including records of deliberations of the Council of Ministers, Secretaries and other officers. However, the decisions of the Council of Ministers, the reasons thereof, and the material on which the decisions were taken shall be made public once the decision has been taken and the matter is complete or over, except for matters that fall under the other exemptions in this section.

Personal information is exempt from disclosure under the RTI Act. There shall be no obligation to give any citizen information which relates to personal information. (This clause was substituted by the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, with effect from 13 November 2025. It removed the earlier public-interest override that previously allowed disclosure of personal information when larger public interest justified it.)

Notwithstanding anything in the Official Secrets Act, 1923, nor any of the exemptions in sub-section (1), a public authority may allow access to information if public interest in disclosure outweighs the harm to the protected interests.

Subject to clauses (a), (c) and (i) of sub-section (1), any information relating to any occurrence, event or matter which took place twenty years before the date of the request shall be provided. If a question arises about the date from which the twenty-year period is computed, the decision of the Central Government is final, subject to the usual appeals under this Act.

Any person who does not receive a decision within the time specified under section 7(1) or section 7(3)(a), or who is aggrieved by a decision of the Public Information Officer, may within thirty days from the expiry of that period or from receipt of the decision, prefer a first appeal to an officer senior in rank to the Public Information Officer in that public authority. The appellate officer may admit a late appeal if satisfied the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause from filing in time.

Where an appeal is preferred against an order made by a Public Information Officer under section 11 to disclose third party information, the appeal by the concerned third party shall be made within thirty days from the date of the order.

A second appeal against the decision under sub-section (1) shall lie within ninety days from the date the decision should have been made or was actually received, with the Central Information Commission or State Information Commission. The Commission may admit a late appeal if satisfied the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause from filing in time.
In any appeal proceedings, the onus to prove that a denial of a request was justified lies on the Public Information Officer who denied the request.

A first appeal under sub-section (1) or (2) shall be disposed of within thirty days of receipt, or within an extended period not exceeding a total of forty-five days from the date of filing, for reasons to be recorded in writing.
The decision of the Central Information Commission or State Information Commission is binding.

In its decision, the Central Information Commission or State Information Commission has the power to: require the public authority to take steps to secure compliance with the Act (including providing access to information, appointing a Public Information Officer, publishing information, changing records management practices, enhancing RTI training, or providing annual reports); require the public authority to compensate the complainant for any loss or detriment suffered; impose any penalty provided under this Act; or reject the application.

If the decision of the Public Information Officer against which an appeal is preferred relates to information of a third party, the Central Information Commission or State Information Commission shall give the third party a reasonable opportunity of being heard.
The Central Information Commission or State Information Commission shall give notice of its decision, including any right of appeal, to the complainant and the public authority.
The Central Information Commission or State Information Commission shall decide the appeal in accordance with such procedure as may be prescribed.

Where the Central Information Commission or State Information Commission, while deciding a complaint or appeal, finds that the Public Information Officer has, without reasonable cause, refused to receive an application, failed to furnish information within the time specified under section 7(1), malafidely denied the request, knowingly given incorrect, incomplete or misleading information, destroyed information that was the subject of the request, or obstructed furnishing of information in any manner, it shall impose a penalty of two hundred and fifty rupees for each day of delay until the application is received or information is furnished, up to a maximum of twenty-five thousand rupees. The officer must be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard before the penalty is imposed, and the burden of proving he acted reasonably and diligently lies on him.

Where the Central Information Commission or State Information Commission finds that the Public Information Officer has, without reasonable cause and persistently, failed to receive an application, furnish information in time, or has malafidely denied a request, given misleading information, destroyed information, or obstructed furnishing of information, it shall recommend disciplinary action against the officer under the service rules applicable to him.

To file a complaint or grievance against a government department, use CPGRAMS, the Centralized Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System. CPGRAMS is a centralized portal connected to all Ministries/Departments of the Government of India and its States. When a citizen lodges a grievance, it is routed to the concerned authority for resolution within the prescribed timeframe. CPGRAMS is also available as a mobile application.
section: How to File a Grievance on CPGRAMS

text: CPGRAMS receives grievances on various issues including service delivery, demand under schemes, queries on programmes, and complaints against malpractices, corruption, or discrimination. Grievances received through physical mode, WhatsApp, or Chatbot are also registered on the portal. To avoid duplicate registrations, only the authority concerned with the subject matter registers the grievance.
section: Types of Grievances Handled by CPGRAMS

text: The timeline for resolution of grievances on the CPGRAMS Portal is 21 days. All efforts are to be made to resolve grievances within the earliest possible time. The status of a grievance can be tracked using the unique registration ID provided at the time of registration.

Grievances are ordinarily resolved within 21 days. However, grievances identified as priority by the system, or where early action is critical, shall be resolved within a maximum of 3 days. If a grievance will take longer than 21 days to resolve, the citizen shall be given an interim reply through an interim Action Taken Report (ATR), which is updated with the final response once resolved. The interim ATR does not go into the feedback process until the complaint is finally resolved.

After successful registration of a complaint, a unique registration ID is generated, which the citizen can use to track the status of their complaint. On resolution of the grievance, an SMS/email notification is sent to the citizen's registered mobile number and email address.

CPGRAMS has a multichannel feedback and appeal mechanism. Citizens can file an appeal through the Portal, Chatbot, WhatsApp, or feedback call center, though only a single appeal may be filed for a grievance. Appeals are examined by an Appellate Authority, an officer senior to the Grievance Resolution Officer (GRO) in the hierarchy, who independently reviews the grievance and the resolution provided. Appeals shall ordinarily be closed within 30 days.

As per DARPG guidelines, the following categories of complaints do not fall under CPGRAMS, as they are covered under separate protocols: RTI matters; court-related or sub-judice matters; religious matters; grievances of government employees concerning service matters; suggestions; and anything that impacts the territorial integrity of the country or friendly relations with other countries.

After a grievance is closed, the complainant has the option to provide feedback. If the complainant is not satisfied with the resolution and gives a 'Poor' rating as feedback, the option to file an appeal is enabled. The status of the appeal can be tracked by the petitioner using the grievance registration number.

If a citizen is not satisfied with the resolution of their grievance, they can provide feedback on the CPGRAMS portal and raise an appeal there. In cases where self-feedback is not available on the portal, DARPG tries to reach the citizen through a feedback call center to confirm whether the grievance was actually resolved. An unsatisfied citizen also has the option to reopen or file an appeal through this feedback call.

If a complaint falls under an excluded category (such as RTI matters, court-related/sub-judice matters, or service matters of government employees), the Grievance Resolution Officer (GRO) can close it after clarifying the rule position to the citizen. Such complaints do not require an Action Taken Report (ATR) and do not go into the feedback loop.

Frivolous, spam, or abusive complaints are also received on CPGRAMS. DARPG has developed AI capability to filter such complaints at the initial stage, routing them to the GRO's spam box. If the GRO validates a complaint as frivolous or spam, it is automatically closed with no further action required, and such complaints do not go into the feedback process.

If a grievance is assigned to the wrong Grievance Resolution Officer (GRO), it must be forwarded to the correct GRO, or to the Nodal PG Officer who will identify the right authority, within 48 hours of receipt. A grievance can never be closed simply by stating that it does not pertain to that office.

If a grievance lacks necessary information to be processed, the GRO must make a genuine effort to contact the complainant (by phone, feedback call center, or the portal's request-for-information feature) before closing it. A grievance shall not be closed on the ground of incomplete information without this effort. If the information still cannot be obtained, the grievance is closed under the category 'Closed due to insufficient information', and the citizen is informed they may file again with complete information.

If a complaint involves multiple issues relating to different Grievance Resolution Officers (GROs), the GRO who received the complaint collects input from the other concerned GROs and ensures a coordinated redressal within the standard 21-day timeline.

Grievances pertaining to schemes of the Government of India are examined and redressed by the concerned central Ministry, even if the scheme is implemented through a State Government. The responsibility for redressal rests with the concerned Ministry, which must seek information from the implementing agency and take a final decision. Such grievances cannot be transferred to the State Government for disposal.

Complaints relating to corruption, bribery, harassment, or any other vigilance angle are examined under the guidelines and timelines prescribed by the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) and the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC), in consultation with the Chief Vigilance Officer (CVO) of the Ministry. If found worth pursuing, an acknowledgement is sent to the complainant. Since vigilance cases are governed by CVC and DoPT procedures, no Action Taken Report (ATR) is required and such complaints do not go into the feedback process.

CPGRAMS also receives suggestions from citizens. Subject-specific suggestions are forwarded to the concerned Ministry division with an acknowledgement sent to the citizen. Generic suggestions with no substance may simply be closed. A GRO is not required to act on a suggestion, and once identified as such, it does not require an Action Taken Report and does not go into the feedback process.

If a corruption or vigilance-related complaint is found to be false, malicious, or intentionally filed, and the complainant is identified as a habitual filer of such complaints, the complainant may be flagged and blocked in CPGRAMS.
